title: Formative Writing: Writing to Discover What You Think
author: Teach Like a Champion
summary: The Teach Like a Champion team describes Formative Writing, a technique from their Guide to the Science of Reading in which students write briefly and informally in the middle of a text in order to find out what they think. They distinguish it from summative writing, where students must already know their argument, and cite Joan Didion's remark that she writes to find out what she is thinking. Three mechanisms are offered for why writing before discussion works: written text stays on the page, writing at about one tenth the speed of speech gives time to reach precise vocabulary, and putting thoughts on paper unburdens working memory so students can listen. Practical advice includes 60 to 90 second Quick Writes and Stop and Jots, tentative language such as ideas and might, and a three-step write, discuss, then stamp and revise sequence.
points: Formative Writing is brief, low-stakes writing used midstream during reading to explore and construct meaning, not to prove a finished argument.
Writing before talking reduces the working-memory load of speaking on the spot and gives hesitant students a written safety net.
Framing prompts as asking for ideas, using might and could, and calling answers working hypotheses lowers the barrier to intellectual risk-taking.
Because every student has captured thoughts, discussion becomes true conversation and teachers can circulate to see whom to call on first.
The suggested sequence is an everybody-writes prompt, a short discussion with note-taking, and then a one or two sentence stamp and revise.
quotes: Instead of asking students to write only when they are ready to prove what they already know, we ask them to write in order to find out what they think.
Formative Writing, by contrast, happens earlier in the cognitive process. It is brief, informal, low-stakes writing used midstream during reading to help students explore and construct meaning.

When we ask students to speak before they have had time to process, we are asking them to perform working-memory acrobatics; recalling text details, structuring an argument, and choosing precise vocabulary all in a fraction of a second.
Because we write at roughly one-tenth the speed of speech, slowing down gives the brain time to access precise academic vocabulary and complex ideas that are still in the process of being mastered.
Frame prompts with words like might or could (“Why might Ralph react so fiercely here?” or “What could the symbol represent?”) to lower the barrier to entry and invite safe intellectual risk-taking.
Hesitant or quiet students have a written safety net to refer to, allowing them to speak with far greater thoroughness and assurance.
By making space for students to “think in writing,” we teach them that writing isn’t just a test of what they already know, it is the ultimate engine for understanding.
